bottom_line: Prices are still rising too fast, and the Fed (the people who set interest rates) is expected to raise rates in December instead of cutting them. That means borrowing money is set to get more expensive, while tech stocks are getting hit hard on worries about AI.

stories.title: Inflation is hot, rate hike coming
stories.real: The Fed's favorite inflation measure rose to 3.8% in October, and core inflation (prices minus food and energy) hit 3.3%. Gas got cheaper, but prices overall kept climbing and spread to more things, while the economy grew strongly in the third quarter. So the Fed is expected to raise interest rates at its December meeting.
stories.you: Higher rates usually mean pricier credit cards, car loans and mortgages, so check what you owe before rates go up.

stories.title: AI stocks get crushed
stories.real: Nvidia led a sell-off in chip and AI stocks as investors worried about how much companies are spending on AI and about higher rates. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down almost 4% in early trading, Anthropic fell further below its IPO price, and money rushed into Treasuries (U.S. government bonds). The Dow later turned positive as Wall Street tried to bounce back.

stories.title: New tariffs on 14 countries
stories.real: The U.S. proposed new tariffs (taxes on imported goods) on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU. Tariffs can push prices up no matter how they're put in place, which adds to the Fed's inflation problem. Gold fell to its lowest level in more than a year as bets on rate hikes grew.
stories.you: Imported goods from those countries could cost more, adding to prices that are already climbing.

stories.title: Holiday budgets are getting squeezed
stories.real: Food, travel, gifts and even toys cost more this year, partly because of inflation and energy shocks from the Iran war. More people are shopping secondhand to stretch their money, and spending may not hold up much longer.
stories.you: Set a holiday budget now, because your money buys less than it did last year.

stories.title: Nvidia and the White House
stories.real: Nvidia brought back CEO Jensen Huang after pressure from Trump, which is drawing criticism from both parties about how close tech companies are to the administration. Records show Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, and Trump said it's 'not too late' for the U.S. to take a stake in Nvidia.
stories.you: Nvidia is one of the biggest companies in most stock index funds, so political news about it can move what you own.
